description_full: QuinStreet, Inc., an online performance marketing company, provides customer acquisition services for its clients in the United States and internationally. The company provides online marketing services, such as qualified clicks, leads, calls, applications, and customers through its websites or third-party publishers to financial and home services industries. It also develops the QuinStreet Rating Platform product for insurance agents and the CloudControlMedia that provides performance marketing agency and technology services to clients in financial services, education, and other markets. The company was incorporated in 1999 and is headquartered in Foster City, California.

CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (4/10).
financial_summary: QuinStreet, Inc. is a small-cap communication services business with a $1.1B market cap on $1.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +31% over the past three years and +16% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at -2% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 11% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $128M in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.62× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage runs at 8.1×.

Shareholder yield of 2.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 3.4% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 47% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Elevated short interest (11.8% of float) — sophisticated money is betting the other way
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $17.4M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Gross margin trails most Communication Services peers — competitors appear to have the pricing hand
Significant goodwill (36% of assets) from past acquisitions — a soft asset a conservative appraisal discounts to zero
Advertising-cycle exposure and content/regulatory risk — a single platform policy shift or ad-spend contraction cascades through the P&L quickly.
Cord-cutting acceleration and audience fragmentation — legacy distribution bundles unravel faster than subscription revenue can replace them.
AI-generated content commoditisation — as creation costs collapse toward zero, content libraries lose pricing power and differentiation narrows.

sect: Its 3% operating margin trails the Communication Services median (9%) by 6pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.13x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+22.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 171 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 11% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 8% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 15% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 61% and a beta of 0.94, it moves roughly with the market.
About $14.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 60% in the 2020 crash and 54% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $12.91 (margin of safety -47%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 29%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $8.78 to $19.55 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Communication Services peers: cheaper on P/E 11.7 vs 15.4 and P/FCF 8.5 vs 11.1, richer on EV/EBITDA 13.3 vs 9.9 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 11.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $25.17 on average, 33% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 19.4% annual cash-flow growth, 7pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 2% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.2%, so growth at these returns destroys value.
It runs a 11% gross margin and converts 10% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.62x.
ROE of 25% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.9% of revenue on R&D and 2.9% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $58.3M (5% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.6, in the safe zone).
The Beneish M-score (-2.09) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
Goodwill makes up 36% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 30.5% over 3 years, 17.5% over 5 years and 15.8% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 31%).
Free cash flow has compounded 21.3% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.1x depreciation (0.3% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 24, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 15.1% on average.
Analysts expect 13.2% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.4%, and institutions hold 96%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (9 sales, net $17.4M sold).
It returns 2.9% a year to shareholders (2.9% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 1.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
Short interest is elevated at 11.8% of the float, 6.0 days to cover.
people: With about 1,074 employees, each generates about $1.2M of revenue, 2.0x the Communication Services median, and revenue has grown 9.3% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $119K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $605K (1x revenue per employee).
